title: Are the High-weight Neurons the Important Ones in Image Classification Neural Networks?

images.desc:
2.2 Selection of Critical Neurons in Model Pruning


Neural network pruning can be categorized based on granularity into unstructured pruning ([36], [35], [19]) and structured pruning ([20], [31]). Unstructured pruning is particularly effective for reducing the memory footprint of neural networks during both training and inference. Notably, neuron-based pruning facilitates a more flexible and tailored final architecture.
Among neuron-based methods, Han et al.([24]) proposed an unstructured pruning technique that identifies neurons with absolute weight values below an empirical threshold as unimportant. These neurons are pruned to achieve a sparse network weight pattern. Similarly, Sun et al. ([40]) pruned non-essential neurons by evaluating weights with the smallest magnitudes, multiplied by the corresponding input activations for each output.
In contrast, structured pruning adopts a hardware-friendly approach by removing convolutional kernels based on importance rankings or similarity. For instance, S.H. Shabbeer Basha et al.([37]) assess filter(combination of neurons) importance during iterative pruning by calculating the similarity between filters. Tianzong Yu et al.([47]) combined the inverse input autocorrelation matrix with the weight matrix to evaluate and prune unimportant input channels or nodes in each CNN layer. This method enables the removal of redundant filters, significantly increasing speed while maintaining a low error rate. Yongbin Z et al.([41]) calculate the importance scores of filters based on their weights, subsequently removing those with low scores considering both their direct and indirect impacts, which leads to improved performance. By eliminating redundant or less contributive neurons, computational costs and storage requirements can be reduced while preserving model performance, thus enhancing overall model efficiency.
The prevailing practice has been to prune neurons with smaller weights([21],[22]), but it remains unclear whether neurons with larger weights truly exert a significant influence. Previous studies have not provided relevant research or conclusions on this matter.

3.2 Analyzing the Overlap Between High-Weight Neurons and Key Accuracy Contributors


In the context of a trained neural network, we adopt a systematic approach to identify critical neurons by iteratively ablating each neuron within the network’s architecture. Specifically, for each layer of the weight matrix, we conduct a granular analysis by sequentially setting the weights of individual neurons to zero. This method effectively simulates the removal of a single neuron while maintaining the integrity of the network’s structure and the parameters of other neurons.


Following each ablation, we evaluate the modified network using an independent test dataset. By measuring key performance metrics such as accuracy, we quantify the impact of each neuron’s removal on the model’s predictive capabilities. Through comprehensive comparisons of the model’s performance before and after each ablation, we are able to pinpoint neurons that exert a substantial influence on the overall output. These neurons are deemed critical, as their absence leads to significant degradation in the model’s accuracy or other performance indicators.


After training the neural network, we take the absolute values of the weights and sort them in descending order, selecting the top n neurons as the weight importance TOP-n set SwS_{w}. We performe ablation on individual neurons and evaluate the network’s accuracy after each neuron is ablated. The neurons with the highest impact on accuracy are defined as the accuracy impact TOP-n set SaS_{a}. Finally, the overlap ratio between is calculated these two sets, which is measuring the proportion of neurons in the Accuracy Impact TOP-n set SaS_{a} that also appear in the Weight Importance TOP-n set SwS_{w}.


An importance quantification metric is constructed to comprehensively reflect the relationship between neuron weight magnitudes and their functional impact within the network:
